title: The covalent model: bonds and shapes
summary: Atoms share electron pairs to form covalent bonds. Draw Lewis structures, use VSEPR to predict shapes and bond angles, and decide whether molecules are polar; at HL, handle expanded octets and formal charge.

keyterms.definition: The electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the bonded atoms.
A diagram showing all valence electrons in a molecule or ion as bonding pairs and lone (non-bonding) pairs.
Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to achieve eight valence electrons; hydrogen and some others are exceptions.
A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from the same atom (dative bond).
The number of shared electron pairs between two atoms; higher bond order means shorter, stronger bonds.
Electron domains around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves as far apart as possible.
A region of electron density around a central atom: a lone pair, single bond or multiple bond.
A pair of valence electrons not involved in bonding; repels more strongly than bonding pairs.
Unequal sharing of electrons in a bond due to an electronegativity difference, giving partial charges δ+ and δ−.
A molecule is polar if its bond dipoles do not cancel, giving a net dipole moment; depends on bonds and shape.
More than eight electrons around a central atom of period 3 or below, giving five or six electron domains.
FC = valence electrons − non-bonding electrons − ½ bonding electrons; the preferred Lewis structure minimizes it.

questions.prompt: How many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom in water?
questions.explanation: O has 6 valence electrons: two are used in O–H bonds and four form two lone pairs.

questions.statement: In a coordination bond both electrons come from the same atom.
questions.explanation: For example in NH₄⁺, the N lone pair forms a bond to H⁺. Once formed it is identical to the other N–H bonds.

questions.prompt: Which bond is the shortest and strongest?
questions.explanation: More shared pairs (higher bond order) pull the nuclei closer and need more energy to break.

questions.text: The number of electron pairs shared between N atoms in N₂ is ___.
questions.explanation: N₂ has a triple bond, N≡N, plus one lone pair on each N.

questions.prompt: Match each molecule to its bond type between the named atoms.

pairs.right: Triple bond including a coordination bond

questions.explanation: CO has a triple bond in which one pair comes from oxygen.

questions.statement: Boron in BF₃ obeys the octet rule.
questions.explanation: B has only three bonding pairs (six electrons): BF₃ is electron deficient and can accept a lone pair.

questions.prompt: Which species contains a coordination bond?
questions.explanation: In H₃O⁺, an O lone pair bonds to H⁺.

questions.text: A covalent bond is the attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the two ___.
questions.explanation: Both positive nuclei attract the shared negative electron pair.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for drawing a Lewis formula.
items: Complete octets of outer atoms with lone pairs
Place any remaining electrons on the central atom
Form multiple bonds if the central atom lacks an octet
questions.explanation: Total valence electrons are distributed so that each atom (except H) reaches an octet where possible.

questions.prompt: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis formula of CO₃²⁻?
questions.explanation: C 4 + 3 × O 6 = 22, plus 2 for the charge = 24.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of NH₃?
questions.explanation: Four electron domains (3 bonding, 1 lone pair) give a tetrahedral domain geometry but a trigonal pyramidal molecule.

questions.text: The H–O–H bond angle in water is about ___°.
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, squeezing the angle below 109.5°.

questions.statement: CO₂ is a non-polar molecule even though its C=O bonds are polar.
questions.explanation: CO₂ is linear, so the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

questions.prompt: Match each molecule to its shape.
questions.explanation: Count electron domains on the central atom, then consider lone pairs.
CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but its bond dipoles are unequal (C–H vs C–Cl), so they do not cancel.

questions.statement: A double bond counts as two electron domains in VSEPR theory.
questions.explanation: Any bond to an atom, single or multiple, counts as one electron domain.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate bond angle in methanal, H₂C=O?
questions.explanation: Carbon has three electron domains and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, about 120°.

questions.prompt: Order by bond angle, smallest first.
questions.explanation: 104.5° < 107° < 109.5° < 120° < 180°: lone pairs compress angles, and fewer domains spread further.

questions.text: In the H–Cl bond, the chlorine atom carries a partial ___ charge.
questions.explanation: Cl is more electronegative and pulls the shared pair towards itself (δ−).

questions.prompt: Which bond is the most polar?
questions.explanation: The electronegativity difference is greatest for H–F (4.0 − 2.2).

questions.prompt: What is the shape of SF₆?
questions.explanation: Six bonding domains and no lone pairs on S give an octahedral shape with 90° angles.

questions.prompt: What is the shape of XeF₄?
questions.explanation: Xe has six domains: four bonds and two lone pairs opposite each other, so the molecule is square planar.

questions.statement: Nitrogen can form an expanded octet like phosphorus.
questions.explanation: Period 2 atoms have no available d orbitals / too small; PCl₅ exists but NCl₅ does not.

questions.prompt: Match electron domains (bonding + lone) to the molecular shape.
questions.explanation: In trigonal bipyramidal geometry, lone pairs occupy equatorial positions.

questions.text: The formal charge on the central O in O₃ (one single, one double bond) is ___.
questions.explanation: Central O: 6 valence − 2 non-bonding − ½(6 bonding) = +1.

questions.prompt: Which Lewis structure is preferred by formal charge?
options: The one with only single bonds
The one with the largest formal charges
The one with formal charges closest to zero
The one with the most lone pairs
questions.explanation: Structures with formal charges nearest zero (and negative charge on the more electronegative atom) are preferred.
Cl has five domains: three bonds and two lone pairs in equatorial positions, giving a T shape.
PCl₅ is a symmetrical trigonal bipyramid, so bond dipoles cancel. The others have lone pairs making them asymmetric.

questions.text: The formal charge of any atom in a neutral molecule must add up to ___ overall.
questions.explanation: The sum of formal charges equals the overall charge of the species.

questions.prompt: Order by the number of electron domains on the central atom, smallest first.
questions.explanation: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 domains respectively.
